source.title: Honeybees disrupt the structure and functionality of plant-pollinator networks

design: Replicated three-year human-induced experiment in Teide National Park comparing pre- and post-establishment periods of up to 2700 managed honeybee hives, with quantitative plant-pollinator networks and paired reproductive measurements in five native plant species.

source_native_results.network_change: beekeeping reduced wild-pollinator diversity and interaction links and disrupted network organization
source_native_results.high_honeybee_use_plants: Echium wildpretii and Spartocytisus supranubius had significantly fewer seeds per fruit during the honeybee period
source_native_results.low_or_moderate_honeybee_use_plants: the same seeds-per-fruit decline was not detected in the low/moderate honeybee-visitation species
source_native_results.distance_gradient: Spartocytisus plants nearer apiaries had fewer seeds per fruit and a much larger fraction of empty fruits
source_native_results.response_heterogeneity: fruit set and seed-number responses were not uniform across the five focal plant species

observed_chain: common beekeeping/network perturbation -> plant-specific interaction exposure -> divergent reproductive responses among co-occurring plant species
claim_boundary: This validates a multi-plant branching state under an experimental island network perturbation. It does not imply that managed honeybees are the causal mechanism behind Izu or Caribbean branching, and the mixed fruit-set/seed-number responses must not be collapsed to one universal fitness coefficient.
